Duration::sign¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

Duration Duration::sign() const;

What It Does¶

Returns -1, 0, or 1 per element (as a Duration, not a plain integer Series), matching the numeric-sign convention — the complementary piece of information to abs, which discards direction and keeps magnitude.

Parameters¶

None — this is a zero-argument accessor on self.

Returns¶

Duration A duration whose magnitude is exactly 1 nanosecond, positive, negative, or zero, matching self’s sign per element.

Examples¶

Example 1. sign() on a negative duration and a positive one, for contrast.

auto neg_fifteen_min = pluss::duration::minutes(-15);
auto ninety_min = pluss::duration::minutes(90);
std::cout << "sign_neg=" << pluss::series::print(neg_fifteen_min.sign().total().nanoseconds()) << "\n";
std::cout << "sign_pos=" << pluss::series::print(ninety_min.sign().total().nanoseconds());

Output¶

sign_neg=Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-1.0000
sign_pos=Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1.0000

sign()’s result is itself a Duration — one whose magnitude is exactly 1 nanosecond, positive or negative — so reading it back through .total().nanoseconds() (not .total().days() or another larger unit, which would show a vanishingly small fraction) is the natural way to inspect it directly.

Notes¶

  • sign()’s output is itself a Duration (not an int Series) — read it back through a .total() conversion (or a comparison) rather than treating it as a plain number directly.

  • pluss::duration::print(neg_fifteen_min.sign()) also works, and prints -0 days 00:00:00.000000001 — accurate, but harder to read at a glance than .total().nanoseconds()’s plain -1.0000 for a value whose magnitude is always exactly one nanosecond.

See Also¶

  • abs: magnitude alone, the complementary piece of information sign discards.

  • clip: bounding into a range, another unary transform.
